scope: How a failed automated test is triaged before anyone fixes it, for any team that tests a product: who triages it, what evidence is gathered first (trace, screenshot, log, rerun history, recent changes), which disposition the failure is classified into (a product bug, a flake, an environment fault, a test made stale by a legitimate product change, or uncertain), what separates each disposition from the others, and how the verdict states its evidence and its confidence. Out of scope: what happens to a test once it is known to be flaky (quarantine, the retry rule, the fix-or-delete lifecycle), which belongs to testing/flaky-test-quarantine and testing/flaky-test-prevention; production incidents (shipping/incident-response); project issue tracking (planning/project-management/issue-tracking); and every team-specific convention of the team the rules were quoted from.
research_type: Technology / software (intent Evaluate; domain test failure classification; method tool documentation, published industry studies and practitioner sources). Technical bar MEDIUM (official current docs; recency), no escalation. Every figure on failure-cause frequency (Labuschagne et al., Luo et al., Lam et al., Gruber et al. via Parry et al., the Google TAP figure via Luo et al.) is scored on the Statistical bar MED-HIGH: the study, its sample, its measure and its result are named in the claim.

questions.text: Best practices: what is current best practice for this topic?
Known solutions: what solutions, patterns, libraries and tools already exist, and how do they compare?
Platform guidelines: what do the platform owners' own guidelines say, for each platform the topic touches (Apple, Android, Windows, web, the databases and runtimes concerned)?
The expert's view: if we hired an expert consultant in this topic, what would they tell us: what to do, what to avoid, and what people usually get wrong?

methodology.method: guidelines/researching/process/research-methodology-and-sources: orient and classify the domain (test failure classification; technology, intent Evaluate), go first to the test-runner and CI owners' own documentation (Playwright, pytest and pytest-rerunfailures, Apache Maven Surefire, Gradle test-retry, Apple Xcode, Android AndroidJUnitRunner, Firebase Test Lab, GitHub Actions, GitLab, Azure DevOps, CircleCI, Buildkite, Jest) and the large projects' own triage procedures (Mozilla sheriffing and Treeherder, Chromium gardening), then the published studies themselves (Luo et al. FSE 2014, Labuschagne et al. ESEC/FSE 2017, Lam et al. ISSTA 2019, Parry et al. TOSEM 2022), then vendors' flake systems (Meta PFS, Datadog, Trunk), then standards for stating evidence and confidence (ODNI ICD 203, Mozilla bug-writing guidelines), then practitioner sources (Software Engineering at Google, Fowler, Wheeler's review of Agans) for what no primary covers; corroborate across independent publishers; record provenance at generation time.
methodology.search_strategy: WebSearch for each runner's and CI vendor's own pages on retries, flaky status, traces, expected failures, test repetition and failure reports; for the flake-classification systems of Google, Meta and Microsoft; for the empirical studies of flaky tests and CI test failures and their author-hosted PDFs; and for sheriff/gardener triage procedures. Every cited page fetched with WebFetch; PDFs saved by WebFetch were converted with pdftotext and quoted from the extracted text. Backward snowballing from Luo et al. and Lam et al. (to Micco's TAP figure, Labuschagne et al. and Palomba and Zaidman) and from Parry et al. (to Gruber et al. and Alshammari et al.).
methodology.inclusion: Primary: the tool and platform owners' documentation (playwright.dev, docs.pytest.org, github.com/pytest-dev, maven.apache.org, github.com/gradle, developer.apple.com, developer.android.com, firebase.google.com, docs.github.com, docs.gitlab.com, learn.microsoft.com, circleci.com, buildkite.com, docs.datadoghq.com, docs.trunk.io, jestjs.io, git-scm.com); the projects' own triage procedures (firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org, wiki.mozilla.org, bugzilla.mozilla.org, github.com/mozilla/treeherder, chromium.org, chromium.googlesource.com); the peer-reviewed studies themselves (author-hosted PDFs); a published standard (ODNI ICD 203); a vendor engineering post on its own system (engineering.fb.com). Secondary, flagged in the trust basis: Software Engineering at Google (abseil.io), martinfowler.com, Wheeler's review of Agans's Debugging, and Parry et al.'s survey where it reports another study's figures.
methodology.exclusion: Team-specific conventions of the team the rules were quoted from (layout, tags, selectors, mocks, output contracts, step budgets, site registry); flaky-test quarantine and lifecycle (other topics); production incident severity; search-results pages and AI-generated summaries; vendor marketing pages; third-party comparisons (Harness, Mergify, FitGap) of vendors whose own docs were not read.
methodology.scoring: guidelines/researching/evidence/verification-and-trust-scoring: Authority 30 + Independent corroboration 25 + Accuracy/verifiability 20 + Currency 10 + Transparency 15, with the Technical MEDIUM ceiling for tool claims and the Statistical MED-HIGH bar (study, sample, measure, result) for every frequency figure; cite-the-claim-not-the-document, independence-before-corroboration (several pages from one publisher count as one), domain-stratified-trust, suppress-unsupported-confidence (single-source and out-of-domain claims capped), provenance-at-generation-time.

summary: Six of the eleven rules hold at their stated strength. Every failure gets one classification from a fixed set: Mozilla's sheriffs look at all failures on sheriffed trees and Treeherder gives each one classification from a fixed list (fixed by commit, expected fail, intermittent, infra, not classified and variants); Labuschagne et al. classified every failure in 61 projects as flaky, a bug in the system under test, or a broken or obsolete test, and Firebase Test Lab and Trunk ship fixed outcome sets. Not forcing a verdict holds at SHOULD: Luo et al. note that a failing rerun 'may be a real deterministic failure or might be still a flaky test', Treeherder keeps 'not classified', Datadog has 'Unknown', and Meta's PFS reports when it 'cannot confidently estimate'. Evidence that states what was observed and a bug that names the observed misbehavior are required by Mozilla's bug-writing guidelines ('Clearly separate facts (observations) from speculations'; describe 'the observed (actual) result and the expected result') and Chromium's ('Copy+paste the relevant parts of the log'). A flake is defined by its history in every runner and CI system read (Playwright, Surefire, Azure DevOps, CircleCI, Firebase). Four rules are unsupported at must-hold strength: an environment verdict resting on cross-test or probe signals is common practice (Gradle maxFailures, Treeherder's pin-many for infra, Firebase's inconclusive outcome) but no source says a single test never establishes it, and Gruber et al. detect infrastructure flakiness from one test's cross-run pattern; a stale-test verdict naming the new assertion, an uncertain verdict naming the missing evidence (ICD 203 supports this at SHOULD), and a 1-10 confidence scale with a 9-10 reproduction-and-mechanism threshold have no source requiring them. 'Triage changes nothing' is contradicted as general practice: Chromium gardeners revert culprits and disable tests, Mozilla sheriffs file tracking bugs, Azure DevOps puts bug creation in its resolution step. The research adds eleven practices: gather the trace, logs, screenshots and history first; rerun on the same revision before calling a flake; never let a pass on retry clear a possible bug (24% of flaky-test fixes in Luo et al. changed the code under test, 94% of those fixing a bug); find the change that introduced the failure; a named triage rotation; separate infrastructure outcomes from test failures; tell a stale test from a bug by whether the behavior change was intended; tell broken from flaky by the failure pattern; reproduce in the failing environment (86% of Microsoft's flaky tests flaked only in CI); state confidence with its basis; record the flake's cause category; and mark a known failure as expected with its reason. Frequency figures: 18% of test-suite executions fail and 13% of failures are flaky, with 74% of non-flaky failures bugs and 26% incorrect or obsolete tests (Labuschagne et al.); 4.56% of Google TAP failures were flaky (a personal communication reported by Luo et al.).
open_questions: Whether triage stays a disposition-only output that files, closes, edits and reverts nothing (the team's rule triage-changes-nothing), or follows the sheriff and gardener practice in which the triager files the tracking bug, reverts the culprit or disables the test; the owner decides whether the cookbook states a general rule or leaves this to each team.

Whether a stale-test (spec-rot) verdict must carry the assertion the test should make now, or only identify the intended behavior change that made the test stale (the change and its intent), leaving the new assertion to whoever updates the test.

Whether the 1-10 confidence scale with 9-10 reserved for an observed reproduction and a stated mechanism is kept as the cookbook's scale, or replaced by a stated likelihood term with its basis and the gaps that limit it, as ICD 203 has it.

Whether an environment verdict may rest on one test's cross-run or cross-machine pattern (as Gruber et al.'s infrastructure flakiness does), or only on a signal spanning unrelated tests or an infrastructure status observation as the team's rule requires.
Whether 'an uncertain verdict names what evidence is missing and what would settle it' is kept as a must-hold check or stated at SHOULD, the strength ICD 203's standard on uncertainty carries.
What the stale-test disposition is called in the cookbook: the team's 'spec-rot', Labuschagne et al.'s 'broken or obsolete test', or another name.

Whether a flake disposition must also open a bug investigation of the product code, given that 24% of flaky-test fixes in Luo et al.'s sample changed the code under test, or whether that question is left to the flaky-test-quarantine lifecycle the flake is handed to.
limitations: The Google Testing Blog posts on flaky tests ('Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them', 2016; 'Where do our flaky tests come from?', 2017) could not be read: the fetched pages carried only their comment threads, not the article bodies. Google's flake figures are therefore cited only through Luo et al. (a personal communication with John Micco) and Lam et al. (Micco's keynote), both secondary for those figures.
BuildPulse's own documentation was not found; only third-party descriptions (Harness, Mergify, FitGap) were in search results, and they are not cited. BuildPulse is therefore not compared.

Buildkite's flaky-test management page did not describe its detection models; the passed-on-retry, transition-count and probabilistic-score models appear only in a changelog search snippet that was not fetched, so only Buildkite's notification of the responsible team is cited.

Apple's 'Running tests and interpreting results' is a script-rendered page; its text was read from the documentation's JSON endpoint, which is the URL cited. No Apple page on flaky-test diagnosis as such was found, and XCTest attachments were not covered by that page.
Firebase Test Lab's flaky outcome is cited from the Tool Results API reference; the human-facing results page does not mention flakiness.

Gruber et al.'s Python study (infrastructure flakiness 28%, order dependency 59%) and Alshammari et al.'s 10,000-rerun result are cited through Parry et al.'s peer-reviewed survey, not from the original papers, which were not fetched.
The ISTQB glossary and IEEE 1044 (classification for software anomalies) were not read: the glossary is script-rendered and IEEE 1044 is paywalled; no claim rests on them.

HTML pages were read through WebFetch's extraction; quotes from them are the extracted text. Quotes from PDFs (Luo, Labuschagne, Lam, Parry, ICD 203) were taken from pdftotext output of the fetched files.

No source found treats an agent or automated reviewer as the triager; every procedure read assigns triage to people (sheriffs, gardeners, test owners) or to tools that label flakiness. The rules are judged as general practice for whoever triages.
Windows has no bearing on this topic beyond Azure DevOps: no Windows-specific test-triage guidance was found.

Second check 2026-11-24: refuted (quote-found no, supports-claim partly): The source reads "and determines if the failure is a regression or an intermittent failure", not "determine".
